title: one full moon, three stories
hook: lanterns, a baby statue bathed in water, temples at dawn: the Buddha's birthday, and more
carry: he was a person who woke up

segments.voice: Yesterday: dana, giving, the open hand that fills the monk's bowl. Today, one full moon that means three things.

Lotus lanterns strung across a street in Seoul. A small statue of a baby, one hand pointing up, standing in a bowl of flowers while people line up to pour water over it. Families dressed in white at a temple in Sri Lanka before sunrise. Many of them will tell you it's the Buddha's birthday. Some will tell you it's more than that. Same festival, told differently. First, a guess.
screen: `LANTERNS. A BABY STATUE. WHITE CLOTHES.` → `THE BUDDHA'S BIRTHDAY?` → `AND MORE.`

segments.voice: Vesak takes its name from a spring month in the old Indian calendar. In many Theravada countries, like Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar, its full moon marks three things at once: the Buddha's birth, his awakening and his death. Tradition says all three fell on that same full moon. In Japan, the birthday has its own flower festival in April, and across much of East Asia his awakening and death are remembered on other days of the year. Different calendars, the same life. The water poured over the baby statue recalls a story: when he was born, streams of water fell from the sky to bathe him. And who is everyone celebrating? Buddha isn't a name. It's a title, from a word meaning to wake up. In one old story, a man follows his footprints and asks: are you a god? No. A spirit? No. A human being? No again. Then what are you? Remember me, he says, as awake. Not a god, by his own account: a person who woke up.
screen: `VESAK — A SPRING FULL MOON` · `BIRTH, AWAKENING, DEATH` · `DIFFERENT DAYS, SAME LIFE` · `BUDDHA — ONE WHO WOKE UP` · then, large: `HE WAS A PERSON WHO WOKE UP.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, picture a single lantern being lit. On the second, bring to mind one person whose life lit something in yours. On the third, let yourself be glad they were here.
Vesak. One spring full moon for his birth, his awakening and his death, told differently in different places. Sixth word.
Your line: he was a person who woke up. That's who the lanterns are for. Day six, done.

howItsDone: On Vesak, Buddhists in many Theravada countries visit temples, keep the precepts, give food, hang lanterns and remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and death together; in East Asia the Buddha's birthday is marked with lanterns and by pouring water or sweet tea over a statue of the infant Buddha, with his awakening and death remembered on other days.

fork.setup: a man follows the Buddha's footprints and asks: are you a god? a spirit? a human being? what does he answer, in the story?
fork.reveal: remember me as awake: a buddha. not a claim to be a god, and not quite 'just a man' either.

original.note: Pali: Vesākha, a spring month; Sanskrit Vaiśākha. Thailand calls the festival Visakha Bucha.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha's birthday.
what it means: in many Theravada countries, one full moon for his birth, awakening and death; other traditions spread them across the year.
what a scholar hears: Vesākha, the month; the Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta (MN 123) tells of two streams of water from the sky at his birth; in the Dona Sutta (AN 4.36) he answers 'remember me as awake'.

story.title: the poor woman's lamp
story.text: The whole city is lighting lamps for the Buddha, the king's by the thousand, and a poor woman has a single coin. She spends it on a little oil, barely enough for one small lamp, and sets it down among the others. By morning every lamp has burned out except hers. One of the Buddha's great disciples tries to put it out, and it won't go out. The Buddha tells him to stop: that lamp was lit with a whole heart.
story.source: the poor woman's lamp, from the Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish; told at lantern festivals in Korea and elsewhere

wrong.myth: Vesak is just the Buddha's birthday.
wrong.truth: in many Theravada countries it marks his birth, his awakening and his death on one full moon; other traditions mark them on different days.

notes: Reworked from day 4 (the Buddha) into a Vesak lesson for the rebuilt week one (audience research: 'Vesak: birthday, enlightenment or death, and why the date and story vary'). Kept from day 4: Buddha as a title from budh, to wake, and the Dona exchange (AN 4.36), and its carry, now 'he was a person who woke up'. Cut: the four sights and the palace story, which camp two tells in full (days 29–34).

Theravada tradition places birth, awakening and parinibbana on the Vesakha full moon; Japan's Hanamatsuri (April 8) marks the birth; in much of East Asia awakening (e.g., Rohatsu, December 8) and parinirvana (e.g., February 15) fall on other days. Korea, China and Vietnam keep the birthday by the lunar calendar. Stated generally; confirm.
'Lotus lanterns strung across a street in Seoul' (Yeondeunghoe) and 'families dressed in white at a temple in Sri Lanka' are given as scenes, not as claims about everyone. Confirm.
Bathing the infant Buddha: the voice links it to the streams of water at his birth (MN 123). Some traditions explain it as the nagas or devas bathing him; confirm the framing.
Dona Sutta (AN 4.36): he says no to god, gandhabba, yakkha and human; simplified to god, spirit, human. Confirm.
Story: the poor woman's lamp (Xianyu jing / Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish); the disciple who tries to put it out is Maudgalyayana in most tellings, not named here. Confirm the source and telling.
